newsitem.title: UK: More yen gains expected amid sky-high volatility.
newsitem.headline: More yen gains expected amid sky-high volatility.

text.p: The Japanese yen's fresh burst higher on Monday is just the latest instalment in a trend reversal that began last month, and all the G7 can do is contain sky-high volatility as the rebound completes its course, analysts said.

Market anxiety about the Japanese unit's new lease of life was intensified overnight by concern the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) - or more specifically the U.S. and Japan - will raise the issue of growing Japanese trade surpluses at its next meeting in Denver, Colorado between July 20 and 22.

Analysts said rising expectations of a Japanese interest rate rise and fresh international interest in Japanese stocks were forces behind the timing of the yen rally. The turnaround in the bilateral current account between the U.S. and Japan in favour of Japanese surpluses provides the underlying fuel.

"This move has a good bit further to go yet," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank. "There are a lot of casualties out there who bought at much higher levels than this in the months leading up to May and who have yet to liquidate positions."

"The Japanese authorities successfully stopped dollar/yen becoming a one-way bet but they may well find themselves in the odd situation of talking it back up again soon," said Burke, who sees the dollar returning to 105 yen before settling.
The dollar fell to a six-month low at 111.80 yen earlier on Monday, down more than three yen from the close in Europe on Friday and down as much as 12.3 percent from the peak at 127.46 set on May 1.
The yen's gains were broad-based and the mark fell to a 21-month low against the Japanese unit at 65.22, down 11.4 percent from May 1.

"I don't think we'll ever see the peaks about 127 (yen per dollar) again," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS. He said he sees the dollar returning to about 107 in the next few months but ultimately grind its way back down to 75 on a trend basis again in the years ahead.

Von Maydell said rising expectations of a rate hike in Japan - seen in the steepening of the euroyen interest rate futures curve - compared to a scaling back of rate rise expectations in the U.S. and Europe were the key to the timing of the yen's rebound. The overnight move was a continuation of this, he said.

Using the Taylor Rule, a formula used by many economists and central bankers as a rule of thumb for appropriate interest rate levels, Von Maydell said Japanese short-term rates should be about 150 basis points higher.
Flying in the face of G7 calls for lower volatility on the foreign exchanges, implied volatilities in the options market have been spiralling higher.

The implied level of volatility on one-week dollar/yen options was a heady 18.00/20.00 percent on Monday, while one-month levels have risen to as high as 14.60/15.10 percent from 8.15/45 percent at the end of April.
While soothing comments from Japanese officials overnight were aimed at containing expectations of future wild swings, none displayed discomfort with the prevailing level of the yen.

Unfettered U.S. criticism of rising Japanese trade surpluses from both U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and on Friday from U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky have revealed similar nonchalance over the level of the yen, regardless of public calls for exchange rate stability.
Burke at Citibank said the sheer size of the yen's rally over the past month may help delay a Japanese interest rate rise, but only until the third quarter or so.

Von Maydell at UBS, on the other hand, said the yen's rise would have very little effect on the need for higher interest rates in Japan as the country remains such a closed economy, with exports only about 15 percent of gross domestic product.
"One of the reasons the dollar and yen are volatile currencies is because it takes enormous shifts in their exchange rates to have an impact on such closed domestic economies," von Maydell said.
An indication of the extent to which short-yen positions were pared back in May was shown in a survey of 93 international fund managers conducted by U.S. investment firm Merrill Lynch.

The proportion of respondents reporting underweight yen positions in May was down to 47 percent from 65 percent in February. But, only 14 percent said they were overweight and Merrill reported a bias to remain short of yen.
It's this continued vulnerability to further yen gains that has many traders concerned about a further snowballing of the move.
